176.question: Which of the following options correctly describes the relationship between a Top-Level VI and its SubVIs?

options.a: The top-level VI is the main VI that runs directly and that calls, within its block diagram, one or more SubVIs
options.b: A top-level VI can never contain SubVIs
options.c: A SubVI must always run independently, never inside another VI
options.d: There is no difference between a top-level VI and a SubVI

176.explanation: The Top-Level VI is the one the user runs directly; it can (and normally does) call SubVIs from its block diagram to structure the code modularly.

177.question: Which of the following SubVI documentation practices is most useful for other developers who reuse it without seeing its internal code?

options.a: Writing clear descriptions in VI Properties and on each control/indicator, together with a representative icon
options.b: Naming the VI only with consecutive numbers, with no descriptive text
options.c: Removing the default icon and leaving it blank
options.d: Avoiding any documentation in order to save development time

177.explanation: Good documentation (a VI description, a description for each terminal, and a representative icon) lets other developers understand and correctly use the SubVI without having to inspect its internal block diagram.

178.question: What happens to the front panel of a SubVI when it is called from another VI in normal execution mode (with no pop-up window enabled)?

options.a: It generally stays hidden during execution, unless explicitly configured to be displayed
options.b: It is always shown automatically in a pop-up window
options.c: The SubVI cannot run if its front panel is hidden

178.explanation: By default, a SubVI's front panel is not shown during normal execution; it becomes visible only if that option is explicitly configured in the SubVI's window properties.

179.question: Which shortcut-menu option on a SubVI icon lets you replace it with another VI that has a compatible connector pane?

options.a: Replace
options.c: Convert to SubVI

179.explanation: The 'Replace' option in a node's shortcut menu lets you substitute it with another compatible VI (or function), provided the connector pane is equivalent or compatible.

180.question: What is the standard file extension used to save a VI in LabVIEW?

options.a: .vi
options.c: .ctl

180.explanation: VIs (Virtual Instruments) are saved with the .vi extension, distinct from projects (.lvproj), custom controls (.ctl) or libraries (.lvlib).

181.question: If you need two inputs of a SubVI to be optional (the user may or may not wire them when calling it), which connector pane setting must be applied to those terminals?

options.a: Configure them as 'Optional' in the terminal's properties (This Connection Is)
options.c: Remove them from the connector pane entirely
options.d: It is not possible to have optional inputs in a SubVI

181.explanation: Each connector pane terminal can be configured as Required, Recommended or Optional; optional terminals can be left unwired when using the SubVI without generating an error.

182.question: Which part of the environment lets you see, in a single hierarchical view, which VIs are called by a given VI (its direct and indirect SubVIs)?

options.a: The 'VI Hierarchy' window (View > VI Hierarchy)
options.c: Context Help

182.explanation: The VI Hierarchy window shows a hierarchical tree of all the SubVIs (direct and indirect) a VI uses, useful for understanding the structure of a large application.

183.question: What is recommended before converting repeated code, which appears in several places in the same VI, into a reusable SubVI?

options.a: Verify that the logic really is equivalent in each case and generalize the inputs/outputs so the SubVI covers all intended uses
options.b: Duplicate the code everywhere it is needed, avoiding creating a SubVI
options.c: Remove the functionality from the places where it is not used identically
options.d: Convert it directly into a global variable, without creating a SubVI

183.explanation: Before encapsulating repeated code in a SubVI, it is worth making sure its behavior is consistent across all use cases and designing its inputs/outputs generally enough to cover them.

184.question: What does a broken arrow on a VI's Run button indicate?

options.a: That the VI has at least one edit-time error and cannot run until it is fixed
options.b: That the VI is currently running
options.c: That the VI has finished running successfully
options.d: That the VI is in advanced debugging mode

184.explanation: The broken arrow is the standard visual indicator that the VI contains edit-time errors (for example, incomplete or incompatible wiring) that prevent it from running.

185.question: Which action lets you see the detailed list of errors preventing a VI from running (when the broken arrow appears)?

options.a: Click the broken arrow, which opens the 'Error List' window
options.c: Save the VI under a different name

185.explanation: Clicking the broken Run arrow opens the Error List window, which details each edit-time error along with a brief description of its cause.

186.question: Which debugging tool lets you watch, in real time and as an animation, how data flows through the block diagram during execution?

options.a: Highlight Execution
options.c: Breakpoint

186.explanation: Highlight Execution slows down the VI's execution and shows animations (bubbles) representing the flow of data along the wires, making the actual execution order easier to understand.

187.question: Which debugging tool lets you view the value of data on a specific wire at the exact moment it passes through that point during execution?

options.a: Probe
options.c: Breakpoint

187.explanation: A Probe is placed on a wire and shows, in a pop-up window, the exact value of the data travelling through that point at each moment of execution.

188.question: Which debugging tool automatically halts VI execution at a specific point on the block diagram, allowing the program state to be inspected at that instant?

options.a: Breakpoint
options.c: Highlight Execution

188.explanation: A Breakpoint pauses VI execution just before or after executing the node where it was placed, letting you examine values and continue step by step from there.

189.question: Which tool is used to place a Breakpoint on a node, wire or structure of the block diagram?

options.a: The 'Set Breakpoint' tool from the Tools palette (stop-sign icon)
options.c: The Wiring tool

189.explanation: The Breakpoint tool, shown with an icon resembling a stop sign, is selected from the Tools palette and applied by clicking the diagram element where you want execution to pause.

190.question: What is the difference between 'Step Into', 'Step Over' and 'Step Out' when single-stepping through a VI that contains SubVIs?

options.a: Step Into enters the SubVI's block diagram to debug it internally; Step Over runs the whole SubVI without entering it; Step Out leaves the current subdiagram and returns to the level above
options.b: All three do exactly the same thing; only the button name changes
options.c: Step Into stops the VI completely; Step Over restarts it; Step Out saves it
options.d: Only Step Into is available when there are edit-time errors

190.explanation: These three single-step execution controls let you navigate the call hierarchy while debugging: entering SubVIs (Step Into), stepping past them as a unit (Step Over), or leaving the current level (Step Out).

191.question: What is the main difference between an edit-time error and a run-time error in LabVIEW?

options.a: An edit-time error prevents the VI from running (broken arrow) due to wiring or syntax problems, whereas a run-time error occurs while running a VI that can in fact execute, generally reported through an error cluster
options.b: Both types of error are exactly the same thing
options.c: Edit-time errors only occur in SubVIs, never in the main VI
options.d: A run-time error always immediately shuts down LabVIEW completely

191.explanation: An edit-time error prevents the VI from compiling/running (it is fixed before running), whereas a run-time error arises while a valid VI is executing, typically propagated through the standard error cluster.

192.question: Which standard LabVIEW VI is commonly used to show the user a dialog box describing an error that occurred, based on the error cluster?

options.a: Simple Error Handler
options.c: Build Array

192.explanation: The Simple Error Handler VI examines an error cluster and, if there is an error, can automatically display a dialog box with the corresponding description to the user.

193.question: Which VI/function is used to combine several error clusters coming from parallel branches of code into a single output error cluster?

options.a: Merge Errors
options.c: Build Array

193.explanation: Merge Errors combines several input error clusters into one, prioritizing reporting the first real error found among them.

194.question: Which field of the error cluster indicates, with a Boolean value, whether an error actually occurred?

options.a: status
options.c: source

194.explanation: The 'status' field of the error cluster is a Boolean: TRUE indicates that an error occurred, whereas FALSE indicates there was no error (although 'code' may still carry a warning).

195.question: Which error-propagation pattern is recommended along a block diagram with multiple chained VIs and functions?

options.a: Chain the error cluster from the output of one node to the error input of the next node, forming a continuous 'error chain'
options.b: Ignore the error cluster and manually check each result with a Probe
options.c: Use global variables exclusively to report errors
options.d: Stop the VI immediately with a Breakpoint every time an error occurs

195.explanation: Good LabVIEW practice is to chain the error cluster between successive nodes, so that an error detected at one point propagates automatically and can prevent unsafe later steps from executing.

196.question: If a node receives an error cluster with 'status' TRUE at its error input, what is the typical behavior of most standard LabVIEW functions and VIs with regard to their execution?

options.a: Many functions skip performing their main operation and simply pass the incoming error through to their output, without carrying out the normal action
options.b: They completely ignore the error cluster and run their function normally without restriction
options.c: They immediately and forcibly stop the entire VI
options.d: They automatically turn the error into a warning and continue

196.explanation: Many LabVIEW I/O functions and VIs check the incoming error cluster: if it already indicates an error, they skip their main action (for example, they do not attempt to write to a file) and simply propagate the error they received.

197.question: Which execution setting, available from the View menu or a toolbar button, lets you deliberately slow the execution speed in order to observe Highlight Execution better?

options.a: The execution speed slider associated with Highlight Execution
options.c: The Icon Editor

197.explanation: When Highlight Execution is active, LabVIEW shows a speed control that lets you adjust how slowly the data flow is animated, making step-by-step visual tracking easier.

198.question: A VI runs with no edit-time errors (the Run arrow is not broken), but when executed it consistently produces an incorrect numeric result. What is the most appropriate debugging strategy for identifying the cause?

options.a: Use Highlight Execution combined with Probes at key points on the diagram to check the actual intermediate values against the expected ones
options.c: Ignore the problem, since no edit-time errors are reported
options.d: Convert the whole VI into a reentrant SubVI

198.explanation: When there are no edit-time errors but the result is logically wrong, the recommended strategy is to use Highlight Execution and Probes to inspect the intermediate values and locate the point at which the logic diverges from what was expected.

199.question: Which of the following is a common cause of a VI showing a broken Run arrow?

options.a: A required input terminal of a function left unwired
options.b: A Boolean control set to TRUE by default
options.c: A free comment added to the block diagram
options.d: A cluster with more than 3 elements

199.explanation: Leaving a mandatory (required) input terminal of a function unwired is one of the most common reasons LabVIEW marks a VI as broken, showing the broken arrow.

200.question: What does a small red 'X' over a Probe placed on a wire represent, after running the VI?

options.a: That this particular wire did not execute/did not carry data during that run of the VI (for example, because it is in an unselected case of a Case Structure)
options.b: That the value shown is always invalid
options.c: That the Probe is misconfigured and must be deleted
options.d: That an irreversible critical error occurred

200.explanation: If the wire the Probe is on belongs to a branch of code that did not execute on that pass (for example, an unselected case of a Case Structure), the Probe may indicate that no updated value is available.
